carryoverIn.title: Nonogram Puzzle Checker
carryoverIn.plainSentence: A picture-by-numbers (nonogram) maker that lets you draw a picture, get its clues, and check whether it can be solved without guessing.
carryoverIn.pitch: Draw a picture on a small grid and the page writes the number clues around it, like a picture-by-numbers puzzle. It then solves the puzzle the way a person would, one row or column at a time, and reports whether the clues have exactly one answer and whether the whole grid falls out without guessing. If it does not, it shades the stuck squares and suggests a one-square change that repairs it; then you print the puzzle sheet and an answer page.
carryoverIn.firstMinute: A 10 by 10 sample picture is already drawn with its clues written around it, and a slow replay is solving it pass by pass in colour. A verdict card reads something like 'One answer, no guessing needed, 6 passes, easy'. Click a single square to flip it and watch the verdict change, perhaps to 'Two answers' with the ambiguous squares shaded.
conceptsToLearn: A nonogram is a picture-by-numbers grid: each number says how long a run of filled squares is in that row or column.
carryoverIn.whyNow: Timeless: anyone who makes puzzles for a book, a class or a friend hits the same trap, a puzzle that has one answer on paper but forces guessing. The page makes that visible in seconds.

purposeDetail.job: Turn a drawn picture into nonogram clues and prove, with visible working, whether the puzzle has exactly one answer and can be finished by row-and-column logic alone.
purposeDetail.audience: Puzzle makers, teachers, parents and hobbyists who want to design nonograms that are fair to solve, and solvers curious why a puzzle got stuck.

paywallEvidence.product: A paid no-guess nonogram toolkit sold through a small-seller storefront
paywallEvidence.whatIsGated: The check that every accepted puzzle can be finished by row-and-column logic alone, plus a print-ready puzzle-book PDF with answer pages; listed at 29 US dollars as of 2026-10-13, per the seller's own listing (never shown on the page).

purposeDetail.freeGap: Free options check uniqueness (a game's maker feature, open-source editors and solvers), so uniqueness alone is not the gap. I saw no free tool that tests the stricter no-guess property, shows each solving pass and proposes a one-square repair, but that is unconfirmed. The remaining gap: private, in the browser, shows its working, suggests the fix. The page names no product.
purposeDetail.oracle: OEIS A391619: the number of n by n grids with a unique solution reachable by row-and-column logic alone is 1, 2, 14, 384, 51234 for sizes 0 to 4 and 24976511 for size 5. The self-test enumerates every grid up to 4 by 4 and compares; the 5 by 5 count is an optional background run. The newsletter's stuck 5 by 5 puzzle is a further case.
purposeDetail.inputs: A picture drawn by clicking or dragging on a grid from 5 by 5 to 15 by 15 (20 by 20 under More), or pasted clue numbers; a sample picture is preloaded.
purposeDetail.outputs: Clue numbers, a verdict (no solution, several solutions, one solution needing guesses, or one solution reached by logic alone), a difficulty label from the pass count, the stuck squares, a suggested one-square repair, and exports: puzzle sheet and answer page as PNG, SVG and a print layout, plus a share link holding the grid.
purposeDetail.limits: Black-and-white nonograms only, 5 to 15 squares a side. Exhaustive checking of larger grids is capped and reported as 'could not decide' rather than guessed. Difficulty is a rough label from solving passes, not a verdict on how hard a person will find it. No photo import.

research.summary: Uniqueness and no-guess solvability are different properties. A seller of a paid toolkit says most nonogram generators check nothing or only uniqueness, while its own accepted puzzles must be finished by working one row or column at a time (seller claim). OEIS A391619 counts n by n grids that are unique and line-solvable (1, 2, 14, 384, 51234, 24976511 for sizes 0 to 5), and the 5 by 5 value is also reported by a puzzle newsletter and a forum thread. A larger unique-solution count for 5 by 5 was relayed by a commenter and is unverified. Uniqueness checking is NP-hard in general, but a line solver is cheap, so an auditable in-browser checker with a capped search and a repair suggestion is realistic in one morning.

facts.claim: As of 2026-10-13 a seller's own listing offers a no-guess nonogram toolkit for 29 US dollars. It says a puzzle is accepted only if working one row or column at a time, filling only forced squares, finishes the grid, and that most generators check nothing or only uniqueness (seller claim).
A nonogram can have exactly one solution and still not be solvable by row-and-column logic alone; a puzzle newsletter gives a small 5 by 5 example where line work gets stuck.
Of the 33,554,432 possible 5 by 5 grids, 24,976,511 give puzzles that are unique and solvable by line logic alone; OEIS A391619 lists 1, 2, 14, 384, 51234, 24976511 for sizes 0 to 5.

Deciding whether a nonogram has a solution is NP-complete (Ueda and Nagao, 1996), and deciding uniqueness of a given solution is also hard, so an exhaustive answer count on large grids needs a work cap; simple nonograms are solved by cheap local line reasoning.

A free game's maker feature uses a solver that rejects puzzles with several solutions, and open-source nonogram editors and solvers exist; no free tool seen in my searches tests the stricter no-guess property with a repair suggestion (not confirmed for every tool).

Self-test panel that enumerates every grid up to 4 by 4 and checks the counts against published sequences
design.scopeForOneDay: Built: drawing grid (5, 10, 15), clue generator, line solver with pass replay, depth-first answer counter with a node cap, difficulty label, single-flip repair search in a worker, SVG and print-layout export, share link in the page address, self-test over all grids up to 4 by 4 plus the optional 5 by 5 run. Cut: 20 by 20 grids, PNG export, coloured nonograms, photo import, puzzle packs, accounts.
risks: The paywall claim rests on one seller listing (its own page, so verified under the primary-source rule, but a marketing claim with no independent review); it never goes on the page and the page names no product.
The 5 by 5 unique-solution count 25,309,575 and the 333,064 gap are unverified (relayed by a commenter); the page leaves them out or shows them as 'as of 2026-10-13, per a forum commenter'.
The OEIS entry was seen in a search result and could not be opened; the self-test relies on terms for sizes 0 to 4, which the other two sources and a brute-force run check anyway.

The self-test must reach 8 known-answer cases from named sources: counts for sizes 1 to 4, the 5 by 5 count and the newsletter's stuck example are 6; the spec must add definition-based cases labelled as such, or report fewer named-source cases honestly.
The free-gap claim (no free tool tests no-guess solvability) is unconfirmed; the page states only what it does.
Brute-force over all 33 million 5 by 5 grids may be slow in a browser; keep sizes 0 to 4 automatic and make the 5 by 5 run an optional worker with a progress bar.

A drawn grid has many focusable squares; it must be one composite widget with a single tab stop and arrow-key movement so the first screen stays within 8 controls and the primary button stays visible at 1280x650.
Difficulty by pass count is a rough proxy; the page says so rather than claiming a human rating.

The 25,309,575 figure and the free-gap claim stay unverified; a line solver, capped counter and flip-repair search fit a morning if the 20 by 20 size and PNG export are cut.

ideas.title: Prime Number Grids
ideas.plainSentence: A lesson that lets you change a number grid's width and see why prime numbers fall into columns and, in a spiral, diagonals.
ideas.pitch: Drag one slider to change how wide a grid of whole numbers is, and watch the primes snap into a few straight columns. Then wind the same numbers into a square spiral and see why the primes pile onto diagonal lines, with every line explained by a small formula you can edit. You leave knowing why the pattern exists, what it does and does not say about primes, and why a formula that is prime 40 times in a row still fails on the 41st try.
ideas.firstMinute: The first frame already shows numbers 1 to 300 laid out in rows of 6 with the primes lit up, and almost all of them sit in two columns. Dragging the width slider to 30 or 7 reshuffles the grid instantly and the lit columns move with it, so the first success (seeing the primes pick columns) needs no reading.
conceptsToLearn: A prime is a whole number above 1 that only divides evenly by 1 and itself
ideas.whyNow: Timeless: it needs no news hook, and a fresh visual proof of a classic fact is as good in a month as today.

purposeDetail.concept: When the whole numbers are written in rows of width w, each column holds one residue class mod w. A prime larger than w can only live in a column whose residue shares no factor with w, so the primes are confined to those columns. In the square Ulam spiral, every straight diagonal carries the values of one quadratic polynomial, and that polynomial decides which diagonals are barren (always even, or factorable) and which are rich in primes.
purposeDetail.whyNiche: The Ulam spiral is shown everywhere as a pretty picture or a mystery, so people think the diagonals are magic or that they predict primes. The simple reason (columns and diagonals are residue classes and quadratics, and some of them are ruled out by divisibility) is rarely shown with a control the visitor can move.
purposeDetail.audience: Curious adults and students aged 14 and up who know what a prime number is and want to see why a famous picture looks the way it does.
prerequisites: Knowing what a prime number is
Dividing whole numbers with a remainder
misconceptions: If a number is of the form 6k plus or minus 1 it must be prime (it only can be: the form is necessary, not sufficient)
The diagonal lines in the Ulam spiral mean primes follow a simple formula that predicts them
A polynomial that gives primes many times in a row, such as n squared minus n plus 41, must give primes forever
purposeDetail.ahaMoment: At width 6 the visitor sees only two columns can hold primes and realises it is just 'not even, not a multiple of 3'. Then they change the width to 30 and 8 columns survive, then wind the grid into a spiral and watch the columns bend into diagonals: the same rule, in a new shape.
demos: Rows of 6: a width slider over numbers 1 to 300 with primes lit; click a column to see why its numbers are never prime
Any width: the surviving columns are highlighted, with a live count of how many columns are 'open' for primes at that width (7 gives 6, 10 gives 4, 30 gives 8)
Sieve by hand: strike multiples of 2 and 3 on the width-6 grid and watch only columns 1 and 5 remain
Wind it up: morph the same numbers from rows into a square spiral, then pick a diagonal to reveal its quadratic formula
Why some diagonals are empty: toggle parity colouring and a factoring check on each diagonal
Start anywhere: choose the number at the centre (include 41) and see a long rich diagonal appear, then step beyond 40 to find where the formula breaks
checkQuestions: At width 10, which columns can ever hold primes larger than 10, and how do you know?
A friend says 91 is prime because it is 6 times 15 plus 1. What is wrong with that argument?
On the spiral, why is every other diagonal empty of primes (apart from 2)?
The polynomial n squared minus n plus 41 gives primes for n from 1 to 40. What is n squared minus n plus 41 when n is 41, and why?

research.summary: The Ulam spiral is well documented: lines in the spiral correspond to quadratic polynomials, no quadratic is proved to give infinitely many primes, and Euler's 41 polynomial gives a long run of primes (a diagonal of 40 when 41 sits at the centre, which the verifier recomputed). The 6k plus or minus 1 fact is a standard residue argument, necessary but not sufficient (25, 35, 49 and 91 are composite examples), and Dirichlet's theorem says primes spread evenly over the residue classes coprime to the width. Several interactive prime-spiral pages already exist, so the angle here is a ladder from grid width to residue columns to spiral diagonals, each step with a handle to move. The 41 polynomial is written two ways (n squared minus n plus 41, often credited to Euler or Legendre, and n squared plus n plus 41, which fails at n equal to 40), so the lesson states both forms and checks them by script. Search-only evidence.

facts.claim: In the Ulam spiral (integers written outward on a square lattice, primes marked), straight lines of cells correspond to quadratic polynomials, which is why prime-rich quadratics such as the Euler polynomial show up as diagonals. Ulam and Gardner both noted this.

Along each diagonal of the Ulam spiral started at 1 the values are all odd or all even and the diagonals alternate (recomputed by the verifier over a 29 by 29 window), so alternate diagonals hold no primes beyond 2; some diagonals are also nearly empty because their quadratic factors. The page verifies each such diagonal by script. Not confirmed by an independent source.

The polynomial n squared minus n plus 41 gives primes for n from 1 to 40 and fails at n equal to 41 because the value is 41 squared; n squared plus n plus 41 fails one step earlier, at n equal to 40 (1681). With 41 at the centre of the spiral a diagonal holds a run of 40 primes (recomputed by the verifier; starting at 1 the longest run in a 41 by 41 spiral is 6).
Every prime above 3 is congruent to 1 or 5 mod 6 (6k plus or minus 1) because the other residues are divisible by 2 or 3; the converse fails, since 25, 35, 49 and 91 have that form and are composite.

Dirichlet's theorem (1837): for coprime a and d the progression a plus nd contains infinitely many primes, and primes are asymptotically equally spread among the residue classes mod d that are coprime to d. The number of open columns at width w is Euler's totient of w (6 gives 2, 7 gives 6, 10 gives 4, 30 gives 8, recomputed by the verifier).

As of 2026-10-14, per Wikipedia (single source): no quadratic polynomial has been proved to produce infinitely many primes. Shown on the page only with that attribution. The spiral's naming for Stanislaw Ulam and its 1963 origin were not re-seen this run and are shown only as 'reported'.

ideas.title: Six Dots Triangle Lesson
ideas.plainSentence: A lesson that lets you colour the lines between six dots red or blue and discover why a one-colour triangle can never be avoided.
ideas.pitch: Six dots, fifteen lines, two colours: you try to colour every line so that no triangle is all one colour, first on five dots (it works) and then on six (it never does). A guided ladder turns your failed attempts into the proof, so the pigeonhole argument feels obvious rather than memorised, and the top rung shows how much bigger the same question gets with four-dot groups.
ideas.firstMinute: The first frame shows five dots in a ring with a red pentagon and a blue star already drawn and the words 'no one-colour triangle here'. A button adds a sixth dot; its new lines appear grey, and as the visitor taps lines to colour them, a glowing triangle flashes the moment one colour closes a triangle. First success: the visitor makes a triangle appear on six dots within seconds and cannot make it go away.
conceptsToLearn: A line between two dots is red (the two people know each other) or blue (they are strangers); a one-colour triangle has all three of its lines the same colour
ideas.whyNow: Timeless: a short, complete proof with a surprising edge (five is not enough, six is), and nothing like it in the build history. It also gives the pool a combinatorics lesson that is not about primes or number systems.

purposeDetail.concept: Ramsey's party problem: in any group of six people, either three of them all know each other or three of them are all strangers. Colouring the 15 pairs of a complete graph on six dots with two colours always leaves a one-colour triangle (R(3,3) = 6), while five dots can be coloured with none (a red pentagon and a blue pentagram).
purposeDetail.whyNiche: Most explanations state the pigeonhole step in one sentence and move on, so learners accept the result without feeling why a fifth dot's colouring escapes but the sixth's cannot. Being allowed to try, fail and see exactly which line closes the trap is what the page adds.
purposeDetail.audience: Curious teenagers and adults with no maths beyond school; teachers looking for a ten-minute proof activity.
misconceptions: Checking a few colourings and finding a triangle each time counts as a proof (it does not; the page contrasts a few tries with the case argument that covers every colouring)
Showing six is enough also shows five is not (the lower bound needs its own example: the pentagon and pentagram colouring)
Red and blue mean friends versus enemies (they only mean know each other versus do not)
purposeDetail.ahaMoment: Pick one dot. It has five lines, and two colours cannot share five lines without one colour getting three. Look at the three dots at the far ends: any line among them in that colour makes a triangle with your dot, and if none is, they form a triangle in the other colour. Every escape route is closed.
demos: Rung 1: five dots with the pentagon and pentagram colouring already drawn; tap lines to try to break it and see that you cannot make a triangle without redrawing
Rung 2: add a sixth dot and try to colour its five new lines without making a triangle; a live hint highlights the line that always loses
Rung 3: pick any dot; its five lines fall into two colour bins and the bins visibly overflow at three (the pigeonhole step)
Rung 4: the three far-end dots light up and the visitor checks the three lines among them, ending in a red or a blue triangle in every case

Rung 5: a quilt view lays the 15 line colours out as a strip of 15 patches; a shuffle button tries thousands of random colourings and shows the fewest one-colour triangles found, which never reaches zero (the page counts it itself, labelled as checked here)

Rung 6: the same question with four-dot groups on 17 dots, shown as a pre-drawn colouring (differences that are squares mod 17 in one colour), with a button that checks all 2,380 four-dot groups and finds none in one colour, to feel why the next case is out of reach by hand
checkQuestions: Pick a dot on a seven-person party. How many lines leave it, and what is the least number that must share a colour?
On five people, colour the lines so that no one-colour triangle exists. Which two shapes do the colours draw?
Why does a single colouring of six dots that happens to contain a red triangle not prove the general statement?
If the lines among the three far-end dots are all blue, what triangle have you found?

research.summary: Re-checked by search in this pass: the pigeonhole proof that six people force a one-colour triangle and the pentagon-pentagram colouring of five dots appear in several independent write-ups (an encyclopedia article, lecture notes, a problem-solving wiki, a combinatorics wikibook). The 17-dot colouring from square differences mod 17, which has no one-colour four-group so that R(4,4)=18, appears in a maths magazine, a course problem sheet and a research paper. The minimum of two one-colour triangles in any six-dot colouring (Goodman's case of six) appears in two documents from one research group; the page also counts it itself. The claim that learners commonly skip the lower bound was not documented and is removed; only the documented point stays: five is not enough is a separate claim needing its own colouring.

ideas.title: Coastline Ruler Lesson
ideas.plainSentence: A lesson that lets you measure a coastline with shorter and shorter rulers, watch its length keep growing, then read off how wiggly it is.
ideas.pitch: You walk a ruler along a wiggly coast, shrink it, and see the length climb instead of settling, while a circle quietly settles to a fixed answer. A live chart of ruler size against measured length turns the climb into a straight line whose steepness is the coast's roughness (its fractal dimension), and you finish by ranking mystery coasts by eye and checking yourself.
ideas.firstMinute: The first frame shows a jagged generated coast with a ruler already walking along it in steps, a length readout, and a slider labelled 'ruler size'. Dragging the slider down makes the ruler re-walk the coast and the length number climb, with a second panel beside it where a smooth circle barely changes. First success: the visitor sees the same coast give a bigger length just by choosing a smaller ruler.
conceptsToLearn: Length can be estimated by counting how many equal ruler steps it takes to walk along a curve
ideas.whyNow: Timeless and very visual: it makes the coastline paradox a thing you do rather than a fact you read, and ends on a number (roughness) the visitor can measure themselves. It is a geometry lesson, not number theory, so it sits apart from the other maths candidates this round.

purposeDetail.concept: A wiggly curve such as a coastline has no single length: the measured length depends on the ruler. For a curve with fractal dimension D between 1 and 2, the measured length grows roughly like (ruler size) raised to the power (1 minus D) as the ruler shrinks, so a log-log plot of length against ruler size is close to a straight line with slope 1 minus D (a plot of the step count instead has slope minus D, so the page says which one it draws). A smooth curve has D = 1 and its length settles; th...
purposeDetail.whyNiche: The coastline paradox is usually quoted as a fun fact and stops there. Few explanations let the learner do the measuring, see why the line on the log-log plot appears, and use its slope to get a number.
purposeDetail.audience: Curious adults and students aged about 14 and up, teachers, and anyone who has met 'fractals' as pretty pictures only.
misconceptions: A coastline has one true length that a good enough measurement would find
A smaller ruler just gives a more accurate number of the same quantity, so the length must level off for every curve
purposeDetail.ahaMoment: On the log-log chart the points for the Koch coast fall on a straight line while the circle's line is flat, and the steepness of the coast's line is exactly the extra wiggliness the ruler keeps discovering.
demos: Rung 1: walk a ruler along a gentle curve and a circle; the length settles as the ruler shrinks
Rung 2: the same ruler on a jagged coast; the length keeps climbing and the visitor predicts the next value before it appears
Rung 3: build a Koch coast step by step and watch each stage multiply the length by four thirds while the ruler shrinks by a third
Rung 4: the live log-log chart appears and the visitor drags a fitted line through the points to read the slope
Rung 5: turn the slope into a dimension and compare the circle (1), the Koch coast (about 1.26), and a seeded random coast whose roughness the visitor guesses first
Rung 6: a 'zoom out, zoom in' toggle shows a real quoted example (Great Britain at two ruler sizes) with the figures labelled as quoted, not measured here
checkQuestions: If halving the ruler makes a coast's measured length grow by about 10 percent, is the coast smoother or rougher than the Koch coast (where halving grows it by about 20 percent)?
Why does a circle's measured length stop changing while a jagged coast's does not?
Why is a log-log chart, not an ordinary chart, the right one here?
Can a curve have dimension 1.5? What would that say about it?

The figure D about 1.25 for the west coast of Britain comes from Richardson's divider data as listed on a university fractals page and repeated in two other results; modern re-fits give lower values (about 1.15 to 1.21 in one tutorial, depending on its version). Real coasts are straight on the plot only over a limited range of scales, and a 2006 paper reports numerical artefacts of the divider method even on the Koch island, so the page must say 'close to' and not 'equal to'.

ideas.title: How Reward Schedules Work
ideas.plainSentence: A lesson that lets you run a simulated learner on four reward schedules and watch which ones keep it pressing after rewards stop.
ideas.pitch: Four vending machines pay out by different rules: every fifth press, randomly about every fifth press, after a fixed wait, after a random wait. You watch a simulated learner (a toy model that reproduces textbook patterns) press each one, read its cumulative record line, then cut the payouts mid-run and see which learner gives up first. A short turn on a hidden machine ends at a clean stopping point, and a chart shows why 'it must be due' is wrong for random payouts.
ideas.firstMinute: The page opens with a drawn vending machine and a simulated learner already pressing its button, a line climbing in steps beside it with a pause after each snack. One tap on 'Pay randomly instead' turns the stepped line into a steady climb with no pauses, and the caption says what changed. No reading needed for that first success.
conceptsToLearn: A reward schedule is the rule that decides which button presses pay out.
A cumulative record is a line that steps up with every press, so a steeper line means faster pressing and a flat stretch means a pause.
ideas.whyNow: Timeless: the one-more-turn pull in games, apps and vending machines runs on these rules, and a visitor who sees the rules at work can recognize them anywhere. Not news-bound.

purposeDetail.concept: A reward schedule is the rule that links behavior to payouts. Ratio schedules pay after a count of responses and interval schedules pay for the first response after a time; each can be fixed or variable. Per introductory textbooks, fixed ratio gives a high rate with a pause after each payout, variable ratio gives a high steady rate with little pause, and fixed interval gives a scalloped pattern that speeds up as the payout nears. Behavior kept up by occasional payouts often lasts longer after...
purposeDetail.whyNiche: Most pieces on this topic either name the schedules in a textbook table or wave at slot machines and call it addiction. Neither lets you see the four response shapes appear, or see what stopping the payouts does to each. Game design talks use the vocabulary without ever showing the mechanism.
purposeDetail.audience: Curious adults, game players and designers, students meeting operant conditioning for the first time, anyone who wonders why some loops are hard to put down.
prerequisites: None beyond pressing a button and getting a snack.
misconceptions: A payout is due after a long dry run, so one more press must be closer to winning.
Paying every single time builds the most durable habit, so occasional payouts must be weaker.
purposeDetail.ahaMoment: After the payouts are switched off, the learner that was paid every time quits within a few presses while the learner paid randomly keeps going, because for it a long dry spell was already normal. The page then shows that on a random-ratio machine the chance of a payout after a long dry run is the same as after a short one, which is why the pull to press once more feels like information but is not.
demos: Rung 1, one machine: a fixed-ratio vending machine pays every fifth press; the learner's cumulative record shows steps and pauses.
Rung 2, same average, different rule: put a random-ratio machine (about every fifth press) beside it and compare the two lines.
Rung 3, rules based on time: fixed-interval and variable-interval machines; see the scallop and the steady line.

Rung 4, the pivot and the fallout: switch payouts off for every learner at once and race how long each keeps pressing; a note says this is a lab pattern shown by a toy model and is less reliable in people.

Rung 5, dry-run check on the random-ratio machine only: run thousands of random presses and chart the chance of a payout after k misses in a row, which stays flat. A note says a time-based machine differs, since waiting longer does make a payout more likely there.
Rung 6, your turn: three minutes on a hidden machine, then a guess at its schedule from your own record, then a summary card that closes the session.
checkQuestions: A machine pays about once every 10 presses at random. You have pressed 30 times with no payout. Is the next press more likely to pay than the first press was?
Which of two learners, one trained on payout every press and one on payout about every 5th press, keeps pressing longer when payouts stop, according to the textbook pattern?
Look at a cumulative record with long flat stretches after each step. Fixed ratio or variable ratio?
Name one natural stopping point you could add to a loop that otherwise runs on and on.

research.summary: Introductory psychology textbook chapters, in several copies of one openly licensed chapter plus an independent explainer, describe the four schedules and their response shapes: variable ratio high and steady and most resistant to stopping, fixed ratio with a pause after payout, fixed interval scalloped. These stay flagged as reported, since this check was search-only and the search summary blended its hits. The partial-reinforcement extinction effect is documented in a journal paper whose abstract, seen in several search entries, says it is well supported in the lab, not in field research, and can flip with how attractive the alternative is. Independence of random trials and the 'due' fallacy are agreed by several independent educational pages. A game design article uses the word contingency for schedule.

facts.claim: Per introductory psychology textbook chapters, variable ratio gives a high, steady response rate with little pause and is the most resistant to extinction; fixed ratio shows a pause after payout; fixed interval is scalloped and the easiest to extinguish. Reported, not opened: show as 'as of 2026-10-14, per introductory psychology textbooks'.

The partial-reinforcement extinction effect is the idea that learning under partial reward is more robust than under full reward. Per the abstract of Hochman and Erev (2013), it is well supported in laboratory studies but not in field research, and in one experiment its sign depended on how attractive the alternative was.

For independent random trials such as a fair spin, each outcome is independent of earlier ones, so a result that has not come up lately is not more likely next time; the belief that a win is due is called the gambler's fallacy.
A Game Developer design article says a contingency, the rule for when rewards arrive in a game, is also called a schedule of reinforcement.
Resistance to extinction after partial reinforcement has been studied in gamblers (a university research record exists for such a study); this lesson makes no claim about its findings.

ideas.title: 10-adic Numbers Lesson
ideas.plainSentence: A lesson with a calculator that lets you add and multiply numbers whose digits run forever leftward, where negatives need no minus sign.
ideas.pitch: Type a string of digits that never ends on the left, add 1 to ...999 and watch every digit carry into zero, so the string is minus one with no minus sign. Then hunt for a stranger number, one ending ...8212890625, by choosing one digit at a time so that its square keeps the same ending, and multiply two nonzero numbers to get zero. You leave knowing that infinitely many digits does not mean infinitely large, because closeness can mean 'the last digits agree'.
ideas.firstMinute: The first frame shows a rolling odometer of nines with a plus-one button already pressed once: every digit rolls over to zero and the readout says 'this is -1'. The visitor taps plus one again to see the string become ...0000 and then types their own digits into the calculator, with the first success being a negative answer such as 5 + ...9995 = 0 reached without reading anything.
conceptsToLearn: Carrying: when a digit passes 9 it becomes 0 and adds 1 to the digit on its left
ideas.whyNow: Timeless: a classic mathematical curiosity that is badly explained as a trick, and a good counterweight to a run of games and gadgets. Nothing in it depends on the date.

purposeDetail.concept: In the 10-adic numbers a number may have infinitely many digits to the left. Addition and multiplication use ordinary carrying, and what matters for a result's last k digits is only the last k digits of the inputs. The string ...999 plus 1 gives all zeros, so ...999 equals -1. Two numbers are close when many of their last digits agree. Because 10 = 2 x 5 is not a prime power, two nonzero 10-adic numbers can multiply to zero, which is why nontrivial solutions of x squared = x exist, such as th...
purposeDetail.whyNiche: Most explanations jump straight to the formal absolute value on a prime, or show ...999 = -1 as a magic trick with a one-line algebra step. Neither lets the learner try arithmetic on such numbers, feel why 'size' is the wrong idea, or meet the composite-base surprise of zero divisors.
purposeDetail.audience: Math fans, curious teenagers and adults who know how column addition carries, and anyone who likes odd ideas. No algebra background needed.
prerequisites: Column addition and multiplication with carrying
misconceptions: A number with infinitely many digits must be infinitely large, or cannot be a number at all, because numbers have finitely many digits
Two numbers that multiply to zero must include a zero (true for ordinary numbers, false in the 10-adics)
purposeDetail.ahaMoment: The visitor presses plus one on ...999 and watches the carry run off to the left forever, leaving zeros. 'Size' is replaced by 'how many last digits agree', and suddenly 9, 99, 999, 9999 are visibly closing in on -1.
demos: Odometer: press plus one on a wheel of nines and watch the carries ripple left, ending in all zeros, so the string equals -1

Infinite-left calculator: type the tail of a number (the page shows the last 40 digits of a number that really continues forever), add, subtract and multiply, with negatives shown as ...9s and a note showing the matching ordinary integer
Negate it: the nines-complement-plus-one rule beside the 'subtract from zero' result, plus 1/3 as ...6667 checked by multiplying by 3
Closeness ruler: pick two numbers and see how many last digits agree; the sequence 9, 99, 999 shrinks toward -1 on a zoom ruler while the ordinary size grows

Idempotent hunt: choose the next digit to the left so the square keeps the same ending; the page shows exactly one digit works at each step, reaching 5, 25, 625, 0625, 90625, 890625, 2890625, 12890625, 212890625, 8212890625

Zero divisors: multiply ...8212890625 by ...1787109376 and get ...0000000000 with neither factor zero; a split view shows a 'divisible by powers of 2' part and a 'divisible by powers of 5' part, and why a prime base would not allow this
checkQuestions: What is ...9999 + 2, and what ordinary number is that?
Which is closer to 0 in the 10-adic sense: 1000 or 10? Why?
What are the last 4 digits of ...8212890625 squared?
Predict ...6667 times 3 before you press equals.
Why can't the same zero-divisor trick work with only 2-adic digits (base 2)?

research.summary: Re-checked by search on 2026-10-14; no page opened (host lookups fail in this sandbox). Two independent course or paper results (Berkeley Math Circle notes, arXiv 1710.08835) give the core: 10-adic numbers have digits running infinitely to the left, ...99999 + 1 = 0 so ...999 = -1, negation is the nines complement plus 1, and 9, 99, 999 approach -1. A different arXiv paper and a mathematics blog give the idempotent pair ending ...8212890625 and ...1787109376 and explain why zero divisors exist (Z_10 splits as Z_2 and Z_5). I recomputed everything with exact integer arithmetic modulo 10^60: both numbers square to themselves, sum to 1 and multiply to 0; each digit of the hunt has exactly one valid choice for 10 steps; 1/3 ends ...6667; 5 + ...9995 = 0. A published dialogue (arXiv 2106.01408) shows the 'a number cannot have infinitely many digits' objection. No study measures how common the belief is; the page presents it as a natural intuition. OEIS and MathWorld were not found again and stay unverified.

facts.claim: In the 10-adic numbers digits may run infinitely to the left; ...99999 + 1 gives all zeros so ...999 = -1; the negative of a number is the nines complement of each digit plus 1; a worked case is ...999942 + 58 = 0 so ...999942 = -58 (Berkeley Math Circle notes, arXiv 1710.08835, Waterloo handout, REU notes).

The numbers ending ...8212890625 and ...1787109376 are the two nontrivial 10-adic solutions of x squared = x: they sum to 1 and multiply to 0 (arXiv 2510.11559 lists longer tails of the same pair; the blog gives a longer idempotent F with F(F-1) = 0). Recomputed 2026-10-14 modulo 10^60 by exact arithmetic.

The 10-adic integers have zero divisors because 10 is not a prime power: Z_10 splits as Z_2 plus Z_5 by the Chinese Remainder Theorem, so a product of two nonzero numbers can be zero; a prime base gives none.

Closeness is measured by agreeing final digits: 9, 99, 999, 9999 differ from -1 by 10, 100, 1000 and so on, so they approach -1 in the 10-adic sense while growing in the ordinary sense (arXiv 1710.08835, Berkeley notes).

A published dialogue modelled on a real classroom exchange has a teacher object that a number cannot have infinitely many digits when ...999 is introduced (arXiv 2106.01408); no study measuring how common this belief is was found.

ideas.title: Browser Fingerprint Lesson
ideas.plainSentence: A lesson that lets you narrow a simulated crowd of 1,000 browsers to one, showing how everyday settings add up to a fingerprint.
ideas.pitch: A crowd of 1,000 simulated browsers sits on screen. You switch on one ordinary setting at a time (language, time zone, screen size, installed fonts, graphics card) and watch the group that looks like you shrink, while a meter counts the bits of identifying information gained. Then the lesson springs the twist that settings are correlated, so naive bit-adding overshoots, and shows why clearing cookies does not touch any of this.
ideas.firstMinute: The first frame already shows 1,000 dots, one highlighted sample visitor, and a banner reading '1,000 people look like you'. One tap on a setting chip and the dots fade until a small group remains, with the bit meter ticking up. First success: the visitor sees a handful of dull settings narrow a crowd to a few dozen without reading anything.
conceptsToLearn: Websites can see basic facts about your browser, such as its language and screen size
ideas.whyNow: As of 2026-10-14, a browser-fingerprinting demo titled 'Fingerprints are the new cookies' (listed on its author's site with a post date of 2026-10-06) was discussed on Hacker News and Lobsters around 2026-10-12 and covered by a news write-up on 2026-10-13, so many readers are asking how fingerprinting works; the underlying maths (surprisal, anonymity sets) is timeless.

purposeDetail.concept: A browser fingerprint is a bundle of ordinary settings; each value is shared by many people, but the combination can be rare. The rarity of a value is measured in bits (surprisal: minus the base-2 logarithm of the share of people who have it), and the bits of independent attributes add up, so a handful of common settings can narrow a crowd to a single browser. An anonymity set is the group of people who look identical to a tracker.
purposeDetail.whyNiche: Most explainers just say 'trackers can identify you' or show a scary single score. They skip the arithmetic that makes it understandable (rarity as bits, crowd size as anonymity set) and the subtlety that attributes are correlated, so bits cannot be simply added.
purposeDetail.audience: Curious web users and junior developers who have heard that clearing cookies or using private windows protects them, and want to see why fingerprinting is different.
prerequisites: Knowing that a website can see some browser settings
misconceptions: Clearing cookies or using a private window makes me untrackable
Each setting I have is unique, so that is what identifies me (in fact each is shared by many; the combination is what is rare)
Bits from every setting can be added up to a total (only true if the settings are independent; correlated ones overlap)
purposeDetail.ahaMoment: Four boring settings that each match a third of the crowd leave only a few people; then the visitor sees that two correlated settings (operating system and font list) shrink the crowd far less than their separate bits promise.
demos: Crowd narrower: toggle one setting at a time and watch 1,000 dots shrink to an anonymity set, with a live count of people who look like you
Rarity as bits: drag the share of people having a value and see its bits (half the crowd is 1 bit, one in 1,024 is 10 bits)
Add the bits: stack independent settings and see that bits add while crowd size multiplies down
Correlation trap: switch on two linked settings and compare the naive bit total to the true joint bits from the actual crowd
Cookie versus fingerprint: clear a cookie and see the fingerprint unchanged, because it is derived each visit rather than stored
Defence trade-off: make everyone report the same values and watch the crowd merge, then see what breaks (a screen size no longer fits the window)
checkQuestions: A language setting is shared by 1 in 8 people. How many bits is that, and how many people in a crowd of 1,024 share it?
You stack time zone (3 bits) and screen size (2 bits), assumed independent. Roughly what share of the crowd remains?
Why is 'operating system plus font list' worth fewer bits than the two added separately?
You clear all cookies. Which of the settings on the screen changed?

research.summary: Hook (as of 2026-10-14): the author's own site lists the demo 'Fingerprints are the new cookies' dated 2026-10-06; it appears as a Lobsters story and a Hacker News item dated 2026-10-12 (via a mirror), and a Gigazine write-up (2026-10-13) describes it. Reported point counts differ by source (about 106 versus over 700), so none is used. A Lobsters commenter said private browsing gave a different fingerprint, so the demo's claim about private windows is contested. The science is old and solid: Eckersley's 2010 study found 83.6 percent of 470,161 fingerprints unique and at least 18.1 bits of entropy, from a self-selected, privacy-conscious sample. Surprisal (minus log2 of probability, additive for independent events) is the textbook measure; a 2020 study measures dependence between attributes with conditional entropy, which is why adding bits overstates identifiability, and a 2026 paper cautions that normalized entropy is a flawed comparison. The lesson uses a seeded simulated crowd with hand-made, labelled shares, never real measurements or a read of the visitor's browser.

facts.claim: As of 2026-10-14 the author's own site lists the demo 'Fingerprints are the new cookies' dated 2026-10-06; it was a Lobsters story and a Hacker News item dated 2026-10-12, with a news write-up on 2026-10-13. No point count is claimed because reports differ.

Eckersley's 2010 study (PETS 2010) found 83.6 percent of 470,161 browser fingerprints instantaneously unique, with an entropy lower bound of 18.1 bits, from a self-selected sample of visitors to a test site that the authors call biased toward privacy-conscious users.
Self-information (surprisal) of an outcome with probability p is minus log2 of p in bits: a certain event carries zero bits, rarer events carry more, and the information of independent events adds.

A 2020 study of browser fingerprint properties measures dependence between attributes with normalized conditional entropy, and a second paper notes that attributes with high entropy separately can give lower entropy together, so correlated attributes carry less joint information than their separate entropies added together suggest.

The W3C Privacy Working Group note defines browser fingerprinting as a site's ability to identify or re-identify a visiting user, user agent or device from configuration settings or other observable characteristics.

Reported, not confirmed: a news write-up says the demo showed the same nickname after clearing cookies, switching to a VPN and using incognito mode, while a Lobsters commenter reported that private browsing produced a different fingerprint. The page may explain by logic that a fingerprint is derived from settings each visit rather than stored, but must not state that private windows keep it.

A 2026 PoPETs paper argues that normalized entropy is a flawed basis for comparing fingerprint datasets of different sizes, so the lesson uses plain surprisal and crowd counts and avoids precise-looking entropy comparisons.

design.coreLoop: Demo, question, aha: toggle a setting and see the crowd shrink, answer a prediction question (how many people will remain?), then reveal the exact count from the seeded crowd; each rung adds one idea (bits, adding, correlation, cookies versus fingerprints, defences).
sophisticationHooks: A seeded simulated population of 1,000 with hand-made, labelled attribute shares and deliberate correlations (operating system with fonts and screen size), so every worked example is exact and checkable by a script
A live meter comparing naive summed bits with true joint bits from the actual crowd, which exposes the correlation trap
A predict-then-reveal question at each rung with an instant result
A defence toggle that standardises values and shows the crowd merging, with the honest trade-off
design.scopeForOneDay: Built: one scrolling page with a canvas crowd of 1,000 dots, six setting chips (five on the first screen, the rest behind More), a bits meter, five short demo sections, check questions and a plain intro paragraph. The population is generated in code from a fixed seed. Cut: reading the visitor's real browser, any network request, canvas or audio probes, per-browser defence rankings. The correlated-attribute demo is the one to protect if time runs short: the seeded population needs two deliberately linked attributes whose true joint count the script computes.
risks: Search-only evidence: no page was opened (WebFetch unavailable today). The hook rests on the author's own site plus a Lobsters page, an HN mirror listing, a news write-up and a digest; the Eckersley figures rest on a mirror copy of the paper and a publisher listing, so the page shows them as 'Eckersley, 2010, self-selected sample'.

The persistence-after-clearing claim is reported by one write-up and disputed in the Lobsters comments (private browsing gave a different fingerprint); the page shows it as 'as of 2026-10-14, per a news write-up' or explains the stateless mechanism by logic only, and never says private windows keep a fingerprint.
Hacker News point counts differ across sources (about 106 versus over 700) and the HN site was not fetchable; the page cites no score and no rank.
Uniqueness figures vary by study and sample; the page calls 83.6 percent a 2010 figure from a self-selected sample, and the simulated crowd is labelled as made up, not a measurement.
Safety red line 7 (no fingerprinting): the page never reads the visitor's own browser; any 'show my browser' extra needs a spec decision and would have to stay local, unstored and unsent.
Entropy numbers can mislead (a 2026 paper argues normalized entropy is flawed); keep to plain surprisal and crowd counts and avoid false precision.
The lesson names the demo and its author only as a cited source in the making-of panel, with no copied text, design or branding.

Eckersley's figures, surprisal and the correlation measure were found again in independent results; the simulated crowd keeps the build self-contained.

ideas.title: Anagram and Hash Commitments
ideas.plainSentence: A lesson that lets you seal a sentence as sorted letters, then see why that fails and how a salted fingerprint fixes it.
ideas.pitch: In the 1600s, scientists such as Hooke and Huygens announced discoveries as scrambled letters so they could claim priority later without giving the idea away. The visitor seals a sentence the same way with one move, sorting its letters, then meets the two ways this breaks: the same letters can be read as a different sentence (Kepler read Galileo's Saturn anagram as a claim about Mars), and a short secret can be guessed. The lesson then swaps the sort for a salted fingerprint (a hash) and teaches the modern idea of a commitment: hide now, reveal later, and nobody can change their story.
ideas.firstMinute: The first frame already shows Hooke's famous scrambled letters and the sentence they hide, with one big button that sorts the letters into a row of tiles. Tapping it seals a sample sentence in one move, and the visitor sees the tiles fly into alphabetical order, then taps Reveal and watches the check pass. First success: a sealed sentence that anyone can verify later, reached without reading anything.
conceptsToLearn: An anagram is the same letters rearranged into another order
ideas.whyNow: Timeless. The constraint of the day is one verb, sort: the first three rungs allow nothing else, so the visitor feels how far a single blunt move gets and exactly where it breaks. Commit-then-reveal is the idea behind sealed bids and fair coin flips over a network, and few people meet it with a story attached.

purposeDetail.concept: A commitment locks in a statement now without revealing it and opens later so everyone can check it. A good commitment is hiding (the sealed form tells nothing) and binding (it cannot be opened as a different statement). Sorted letters are weak on both counts: they leak the length and letter counts and fit more than one sentence. A hash of the statement plus a secret random value (a salt) is the standard modern construction; the committer later reveals both so anyone can recompute the hash. B...
purposeDetail.whyNiche: Explanations of commitments usually start from hash functions and mathematical definitions, so learners meet the words hiding and binding with no felt example. Here the failures come first and are concrete: an anagram leaks letter counts, fits more than one sentence, and a short guessable secret is cracked by trying every candidate. The fix is only motivated after the visitor has been hurt by each failure.
purposeDetail.audience: Curious non-experts, students and developers who have heard of hashes or commit-reveal but never felt why a salt is needed or what binding means.
prerequisites: Reading a short English or Latin sentence
misconceptions: An anagram pins down one meaning, when the same letters can usually be read as other sentences, so it does not bind its author to one claim.
A fingerprint (hash) of a short or guessable secret is secret by itself, when anyone can hash every candidate and compare; a random salt is what stops this.
purposeDetail.ahaMoment: The visitor tries to open the same sealed letters as two different sentences (Galileo's reading and Kepler's reading) and both pass the check. Then the same two sentences get different salted fingerprints, so only one can ever be opened. The sort could not bind them, the fingerprint can.
demos: Rung 1, seal: one button sorts the letters of a sample sentence into tiles (Hooke's 'ut tensio sic vis' is preloaded); Reveal checks that the letters match.

Rung 2, who did you mean: Galileo's and Kepler's Latin readings of the same 37 letters both pass the check (Latin u and v treated as one letter), plus a few English look-alike pairs, so binding fails.
Rung 3, what the sort leaks: a letter-count strip and a bundled list of about 40 famous science phrases that narrows as the visitor learns the length and counts, so hiding is weak.
Rung 4, a fingerprint instead: a SHA-256 fingerprint of the sentence; change one letter and watch the whole fingerprint change; the two readings now have different fingerprints.

Rung 5, crack it and fix it: unsalted fingerprints of one-word secrets are cracked live by trying a bundled word list; adding a typed salt makes the same attack fail, and the visitor sees why real salts are long and random.
checkQuestions: Two people claim different sentences from the same sorted letters. Whose claim wins, and what does that tell you about binding?
Why does a fingerprint of the single word 'yes' or 'no' hide nothing, even though hashes are one-way?
What exactly must the committer publish at reveal time so a stranger can verify the fingerprint?
Which property fails if the secret is revealed too early, hiding or binding?

facts.claim: Galileo's 1610 scrambled Latin announcement is usually given as 'Altissimum planetam tergeminum observavi' (Saturn seen as threefold); Kepler read the same jumble as 'Salve umbistineum geminatum Martia proles', taken to mean Mars has two moons. Both use the same letters when Latin u and v count as one (script check 2026-10-14); they differ by one character if u and v are kept apart.

Hooke's spring-law anagram is printed as ceiiinosssttuu (sorted letters of 'ut tensio, sic vis'), first published in 1676 in Descriptions of Helioscopes with the solution given in 1678 per two results; a third result prints 1677 and some copies end in v, so the page says 'reported' and states no single date as settled.

Huygens published an anagram in 1656 to secure priority for his Saturn finding while delaying his book, and gave the solution (a thin flat ring, not touching, inclined to the ecliptic) in Systema Saturnium in 1659 per Linda Hall Library; one result dates his earlier letter revealing it to 1658. Unverified: second support was blended.

A standard hash commitment is commit(m, r) = H(r followed by m); opening reveals m and r so a verifier recomputes the hash. Lecture notes from MIT, Purdue and Stanford agree; hiding comes from the random r and binding from collision resistance of the hash.

Without a random value, a hash of a message from a small set can be broken by hashing every candidate and comparing, so it does not hide the message; the random value is what provides hiding (Purdue slides and MIT notes).

Hash commitments are computationally binding, not perfectly binding: binding holds as long as the hash has no known collisions, and a scheme cannot be both statistically hiding and statistically binding (MIT lecture notes, Stanford notes).

design.coreLoop: Demo, question, aha. Each rung gives one thing to do (seal, open two ways, narrow the candidates, change a letter, crack then salt), then one check question whose answer the visitor can test on the page before moving up. The constraint of one verb (sort) governs rungs 1 to 3 and is lifted at rung 4 as the payoff: a new verb, fingerprint.
sophisticationHooks: Rung 2 uses real history: the same 37 Latin letters genuinely open as two sentences, computed live from the text so the tiles can be dragged between the two readings.

A small hand-written SHA-256 (tested against published test vectors) so the fingerprint works offline even where the browser's own crypto is unavailable, with a one-letter-change avalanche view that highlights the differing bits.

A live attacker on rung 5 that tries a bundled word list, shows hashes per second and then fails against the salted version, with the salt typed by the visitor (no random numbers anywhere, so every result is repeatable).
A 'real life' panel that states honestly what real systems add (long random salts, stronger constructions) and what this toy skips.
design.scopeForOneDay: Built: one page with five rungs, a tile-sorting animation (with a stepped reduced-motion twin), the pure functions (sort-seal, u/v folding, letter-count filter, SHA-256, crack loop) with tests, about 40 hand-written science phrases and a 300-word list, a short history strip with 'reported' dating, an intro and an explainer. Cut: anything that fetches live data, other schemes (Merkle trees, coin-flip protocols), saved progress on a server, sound. If time runs short, drop rung 3's phrase-narrowing and keep seal, ambiguity, fingerprint, crack-and-salt.
risks: The 37-letter string Galileo sent was never read on a page in this check; the page derives its tiles by sorting the Latin sentences and labels them 'as commonly transcribed' instead of quoting a printed string.
Hooke's anagram date is reported as 1676 with solution 1678 by two results, 1677 by a third, and a variant spelling ends in v: the page shows 'reported' and states no single date as settled.

The Huygens story is verified:false (one clear result, second support blended): the page words it as 'as of 2026-10-14, per Linda Hall Library' or leaves out the dates, and does not reproduce his letter string.
Binding is only computational for a hash: the page says 'binding as long as the hash has no known collisions' and avoids the word perfect.

A salted-hash demo can read like password-storage advice: the page says it is not advice, never takes a real secret, uses a plain text field (not a password field) and a visible note not to type a real secret.
A hand-written SHA-256 needs a self-test against published test vectors (for example the standard 'abc' vector in FIPS 180-4) before it is trusted on the page.
Constraint theatre could hide the teaching: the intro names the literal topic (commitments) first and explains the one-verb rule in one line.

verification.notes: Galileo/Kepler and the commitment construction are each agreed by independent results (two sites; three course sites) and the letter claims were script-checked; Hooke dates are 'reported' and the Huygens story stays unverified. Buildable in a morning with pure functions and a hand-written SHA-256.

ideas.title: B-Tree vs LSM Tree
ideas.plainSentence: A lesson with two small database engines side by side that lets you stream in keys and count every page each engine writes and reads.
ideas.pitch: Keys stream into two tiny storage engines at once. A B-tree finds the page a key belongs to and rewrites that whole page, while an LSM tree holds writes in a memory waiting room, flushes them as sorted runs and merges runs later. Live counters for pages written and pages read show who pays where, and a Compact control lets the visitor watch levels merge, so they leave knowing why no engine is free. All counts come from the page's own simplified simulation, not from a real database.
ideas.firstMinute: The page opens with both engines already ingesting a sample stream of 20 keys, and two running tallies of pages written and pages read side by side. In the first 30 seconds the visitor sees one key light up the page it rewrites in the B-tree, and the same key sit in memory in the LSM tree. The first success is watching the write counters diverge, with no reading needed.
conceptsToLearn: A key-value store keeps values that you look up by key
Disks read and write data in whole fixed-size pages
ideas.whyNow: Timeless: engineers choose between B-tree and LSM-based databases every week, and most explanations show only finished diagrams where the costs stay invisible.

purposeDetail.concept: A B-tree storage engine finds the leaf page a key belongs to and rewrites that whole fixed-size page in place, splitting pages when they fill. An LSM tree buffers writes in a memory table, flushes it as an immutable sorted run, and later merges runs into larger levels in a step called compaction. Both engines pay: the B-tree in whole-page rewrites per small write, the LSM tree in repeated rewrites during compaction (write amplification) and in checking several runs on reads (read amplification).
purposeDetail.whyNiche: Most explanations show a finished tree diagram or a table of pros and cons, so the costs stay invisible: nobody sees one small write turn into many bytes rewritten, or a read fan out across several runs.
purposeDetail.audience: Programmers who must pick or tune a database and have heard 'LSM is for writes, B-tree is for reads' without seeing why.
prerequisites: What a key and a value are
That disks and SSDs read and write in blocks called pages
misconceptions: A write happens once, at its final place on disk (compaction rewrites the same data several times).
An in-place B-tree update is cheap because it touches only the changed record (the whole page is rewritten).
LSM writes are cheap because they are sequential, so there is no hidden cost (compaction and multi-run reads pay later).
purposeDetail.ahaMoment: The visitor bursts a second wave of keys into both engines and watches the counters cross: the LSM tree wrote little at first, then compaction rewrites the same keys again and again, while the B-tree rewrote a whole page per tiny update. Every engine pays somewhere, and the choice is only about where.
demos: Rung 1, the familiar: a sorted shelf of index cards. Insert one key and see why sorted order helps lookups.
Rung 2, B-tree: stream keys in; each one finds its leaf page and the whole page lights up as rewritten; watch a page split when full and count pages written.
Rung 3, LSM tree: the same keys enter a memory waiting room (the memtable); when it fills it flushes as one sorted run; counters show far fewer page writes so far.
Rung 4, the read side: look up a key and count pages checked in each engine; the LSM tree may check several runs, with a Bloom-filter switch that skips runs.
Rung 5, compaction: press Compact and watch runs merge into the next level, rewriting keys that were already written; the amplification ratio counter climbs.
Rung 6, the dials: choose a workload (random keys, sequential keys, overwrites of hot keys) and a size ratio, and see which engine pays where; page size stays fixed in the simulation.
checkQuestions: You overwrite the same key 100 times. Roughly how many times is that key's data written in each engine, and where?
Why can a read in the LSM tree touch more pages than a read in the B-tree?
What does compaction buy, and what does it cost?
Which workload would make you pick each engine?

facts.claim: The LSM-tree paper by O'Neil, Cheng, Gawlick and O'Neil appeared in Acta Informatica 33(4), pages 351 to 385, in 1996; its abstract describes deferring and batching index changes in memory and cascading them to disk components, saving disk-arm movement compared with B-trees for insert-heavy workloads.

Per Cassandra's documentation, compaction reads several small sorted tables, merges them, processes updates and deletes, and writes a new table, which is a source of write amplification; reads merge disk tables with the memtable and use Bloom filters to skip tables that cannot hold the key.

An access method that bounds two of read, update and memory overheads forces a lower bound on the third (the RUM conjecture, EDBT 2016); B-trees are usually described as read-friendly and level-based LSM trees as update-friendly at some cost to reads.

Reported, unverified: in a B-tree a small record update rewrites its whole fixed-size page and a full page splits into several writes, so write amplification grows with page size (TiKV comparison page, via search summaries). The page's simulation defines this behaviour itself with 4 keys per page.

As of 2026-10-14, per a third-party mirror of RocksDB documentation, leveled compaction with a size ratio of 10 is roughly 10 to 30 times write amplification; the scout's 20 to 30 times from the RocksDB blog was not found again. A rough model is size ratio times (levels minus one).
As of 2026-10-14, per one benchmark write-up, random-key writes gave about 4.56 times write amplification and sequential keys about 1.03 times, so amplification depends heavily on key order.

design.coreLoop: Demo, question, aha: pick a workload, stream keys into both engines, watch the page-written and page-read counters, then predict the next number before pressing Compact or Look up. The loop stays interesting because each workload (random, sequential, hot overwrites) shifts which engine pays and where, and the visitor's guess is scored against the simulation.
sophisticationHooks: Both engines are simulated in plain code with a fixed small page size (say 4 keys per page), so every count is exact and checkable by a script against hand-worked examples.
Animated pages: a rewritten page flashes, a split pulls apart, runs slide down levels and merge, with a reduced-motion twin that steps instead of animating.
A running 'write amplification' and 'read amplification' dial for each engine, plus a ledger chart over time that makes the compaction spikes visible.
Predict-then-reveal check questions and three workload presets that end in the aha: the counters cross.
design.scopeForOneDay: Build: a deterministic B-tree simulator (insert, split, lookup) and a leveled LSM simulator (memtable, flush, level merge) with page counters, 4 keys per page; SVG rendering side by side; three workload presets, play, step and compact controls; intro, explainer and four check questions. Stretch only if time remains: Bloom-filter switch and a size-ratio dial. Cut: deletes and tombstones, tiered compaction, page-size dial, concurrency, crash recovery, real timing or hardware claims, persistence.
risks: The B-tree whole-page rewrite fact and every amplification multiplier are unverified (blended summaries, single third-party pages): the page defines its own simplified model and shows reported figures only as 'as of 2026-10-14, per <source>' or omits them.
The 'a write happens once' misconception is not documented as a widely held belief by any source seen: the page frames it as a common assumption to test, not as a survey finding.
The aha 'the counters cross' depends on tuned presets: the simulators need scripted tests that confirm the crossing for the overwrite and burst presets, otherwise the claim is reworded.
Simulated counts depend on page size and size ratio and are not benchmarks: the page says so plainly and never claims real database speeds.
Scope is tight for one morning (two engines plus animation): build and test both simulators first, with a stepped reduced-motion twin instead of animation if time runs short.

The RocksDB blog, Aerospike, candost and one other blog source from the scout were not found again and are dropped; the page cites only the Springer paper, the Cassandra documentation and the RUM page as verified.

verification.notes: The LSM paper, Cassandra compaction behaviour and the RUM trade-off rest on primary pages; the B-tree page-rewrite cost and all multipliers stay unverified and are demoted to the page's own labelled simulation. Feasible only with the shrunk scope (leveled LSM, fixed page size).

ideas.title: Cricket Rain Rule
ideas.plainSentence: A lesson that lets you interrupt a cricket innings with rain and see how overs and wickets set the revised target.
ideas.pitch: A lesson on why cricket's rain rule does not simply scale the target by overs lost. The visitor interrupts a sample chase with a rain delay, watches a naive overs-only target and a resource-ledger target pull apart, then sees how the older average-run-rate and 1992 rules behaved on the same innings. They leave able to explain why wickets in hand are a second budget and to predict which way a revised target will move, using a labelled teaching model rather than the official table.
ideas.firstMinute: The first frame already shows a sample chase (first side 280 from 50 overs, chasing side 120 for 2 after 20 overs) with rain at over 20, two bars labelled simple scaling and resource ledger, and a worked revised target for each. A single slider for overs lost moves both bars at once; the first success is seeing the two targets disagree as the slider moves, with no reading needed.
conceptsToLearn: In a one-day match each side bats once, and the second side chases the first side's total
A batting side spends two things: its overs and its ten wickets
ideas.whyNow: Timeless: rain interrupts matches every season and the revised target is the most argued-about number in the sport; the idea is a stable piece of statistics, not news.

purposeDetail.concept: A limited-overs innings is a budget of two resources, overs remaining and wickets in hand. A rain delay removes part of that budget, and the revised target is the first side's score scaled by the ratio of the two sides' remaining resource percentages, not by overs alone.
purposeDetail.whyNiche: Broadcast explainers state the rule in one sentence (wickets and overs both count) and then show a number nobody can reproduce. The ICC publishes the formula and a resource table for the Standard Edition, but few people see how the table is built or why it is not proportional to overs.
purposeDetail.audience: Cricket fans and curious non-fans who have heard 'DLS' on a rain-hit broadcast and want to know why the target is the number it is.
prerequisites: Know that in a one-day match each side bats once and the second side chases the first side's total
misconceptions: A shortened match just scales the target by the fraction of overs lost, like cutting a recipe in half
Wickets in hand matter little; only the overs left decide how many runs a side can still make
An interruption costs both situations the same, whenever it happens and however many wickets are down
purposeDetail.ahaMoment: Two chasing sides with the same number of overs left are worth very different amounts when one has all ten wickets and the other has three: the ledger shows resources, not time, and a rain delay costs more when you have more wickets to lose.
demos: Simple scaling: a slider for overs lost, and the naive target that cuts the chase in proportion to overs
Two budgets: a two-axis ledger of overs left against wickets lost, a percentage in each cell, and the visitor picks cells to compare
Same overs, different wickets: two chasers with equal overs left and different wickets down, and the runs each is expected to add
The interruption: choose when rain arrives and how many overs it takes, and see resources lost, the ratio, and the revised target next to the naive one
The older rules: the average run rate rule and the discard-the-weakest-overs rule applied to the same innings, with the 1992 semi-final replay shown as reported
checkQuestions: Rain removes 10 overs. In the page's teaching model, is the revised target cut more when the chasing side is 2 down or 7 down at that moment, and why?
Two sides each have 25 overs left. Which has more resources: the one with 0 wickets lost or 5 wickets lost?
If the first side's resources are 100 percent, the chasing side's are 80 percent and the first side scored 250, what is the revised target (the formula adds 1 to the scaled score)?
Why does discarding the first side's least productive overs punish a bowling side that bowled well?

research.summary: Re-checked by search on 2026-10-14; no page opened. The ICC's own documents (methodology paper, media explainer, a D/L adjustment paper, all on icc-cricket.com domains) state the core: revised targets follow the two sides' run-scoring resources, which depend on overs to go and wickets down and are not in proportion to overs; a single table gives resource percentages; for the Standard Edition the revised target is the first score times R2 over R1, plus 1, rounded down. The older average-run-rate method is described there as proportional to overs. Two scorecard sites confirm the 22 March 1992 Sydney semi-final; the 22 versus 21 runs off one ball figure is disputed between accounts. Correction to the scout: the table is published for the Standard Edition, so the page's own model is a teaching approximation, not a stand-in for secret data. The fitted parameters of the Professional Edition are reported undisclosed by an arXiv paper (blended summary, unverified). Table cells from an older reference page differ from a later edition (77.1 versus 75.1 percent for 30 overs left, none lost), so cells are shown as edition-specific.

facts.claim: Per ICC documents (Standard Edition): every full innings starts at 100 percent of resources; one table gives the percentage left for any overs-to-go and wickets-lost; resources lost in a stoppage equal the table value at the stoppage minus the value at resumption.

Per the ICC methodology notes: the revised target is not in proportion to the overs each side receives but follows the run-scoring resources each side has, which depend on overs to go and wickets down; the older average run rate method corrects in direct proportion to overs.

Per the ICC methodology notes, when the chasing side's resources R2 are lower than the first side's R1, the revised target is the first side's score S times R2 over R1, plus 1, rounded down; when R2 is higher the extra resources are valued at an average score G50 (245 in the current document, 235 in an older explainer).
England played South Africa in the second semi-final of the 1992 World Cup at Sydney on 22 March 1992 (two independent scorecard sites).

Reported, disputed: the rain rule used at the 1992 semi-final removed the first side's least productive overs (maidens included), leaving South Africa needing 22 off 1 ball by one account and 21 off 1 by another. The page shows the range.

As of 2026-10-14, per an older reference page, resource cells include 100.0 percent (50 overs left, none lost), 77.1 (30 left, none lost), 58.9 (20 left, none lost) and 54.0 (20 left, two lost); a later-edition table gives 75.1 for 30 left, none lost, so values depend on the edition.

As of 2026-10-14, per an arXiv paper, the Professional Edition's fitted parameters were not disclosed (commercial confidentiality), and the published model has the form of an exponential saturation in overs for each number of wickets lost.

design.coreLoop: Demo, question, aha: the visitor changes when rain arrives and how long it lasts, sees the ledger of overs and wickets, the resource ratio and two revised targets, then answers a prediction question (which way will the target move?) before the page reveals the answer, and moves up the ladder to the 1992 replay.
sophisticationHooks: A heat-map ledger of resources by overs left and wickets lost that the visitor can read like a table and probe by clicking cells
Three rules applied to the same invented over-by-over innings side by side: simple scaling, discard-the-weakest-overs, and the resource ratio
A predict-then-reveal question after each demo, with the page showing the reasoning
A transparent model panel: the formula, the five reported anchor cells, and how far the page's own table sits from them
design.scopeForOneDay: One page: an own illustrative resource model fitted by a small build-time script to the reported anchor cells and checked for monotonicity in overs and wickets; five demos (simple scaling, two budgets ledger, same overs different wickets, the interruption, older rules with a 1992 replay shown as reported); four check questions with page-computed answers; the ICC formula with +1 for the revised target. Cut: Twenty20 and per-ball tables, the Professional Edition's score-dependent resources, live data, saved state, any claim of being an official calculator.
risks: The page's resource table is its own teaching model (a saturating exponential per wicket count, checked for monotonicity), not the ICC table: it says so plainly, never presents its targets as official, and points to the ICC's published table and formula.

The anchor cells come from one old reference page and differ from a later edition: they are shown as 'as of 2026-10-14, per that page' with the model's error against them; the 7.0 anchor from the scout is not used.

The 1992 final figure is disputed (22 versus 21 off one ball): the page shows the range and states only what the sources agree on, that the rule discarded the first side's least productive overs and maidens.

The formula's second branch (when the chasing side has more resources) needs an average score that differs between ICC documents (245 versus 235): the lesson keeps to the lower-resource case or labels the value as an assumption.
Check question 3 now matches the ICC formula: 250 times 0.8 equals 200, plus 1 gives a revised target of 201; the earlier wording left out the +1.
The Professional Edition parameter claim is unverified (blended summary): the page does not state it as fact, or shows it as 'as of 2026-10-14, per an arXiv paper'.

Cricket is unfamiliar to many visitors; the first frame teaches 'a side has overs and wickets to spend' with a sample chase and no jargon. The ICC is cited by name as a source only, with no logo or branding, and no person names are in the title.

verification.notes: The resource concept and the target formula are stated by ICC documents on the official domain and by independent results; model anchors and the 1992 figure stay flagged, and the scout's claim that no table is public was corrected.
